docs.title: Gofra
docs.text:
Beta

Gofra is in beta. The language and toolchain may change.

Recreational programming

Gofra is not competing with other languages. It is another incomplete language, much like the others.

A Stack-based compiled programming language.

Gofra is a concatenative (stack-based) language that compiles to native code. Programs are written in Reverse Polish notation: operations follow their operands (2 + 2 is 2 2 +).

docs.title: Quick start
docs.text:
#include "std"

func void main[]
    "Hello, World!" println
end

docs.title: Features
docs.text:
• Native - Compiles to native machine code
  • C-like - Close to C, but has a few more high-level abstraction (for in, type generics)
  • C FFI - Seamless integration with C-FFI libraries
  • Low-level - Write unsafe, low-level code with direct memory access
  • Type System - Validate types at compile time, has compile-time warnings (Partial generics supports, typechecker)
  • Library - By default has support for math, random, network and other libraries
  • First class functions - Has support, and lambda definitions (no closures/capturing yet)

docs.title: Showcase
docs.text:
• Pong Game (examples/03_pong.gof)
  • Simple HTTP server (examples/04_http_server.gof)

docs.title: Platform support
docs.text:
Gofra currently supports native compilation (no cross-compilation yet). Compile on the same platform as your target.

Platform Status AArch64 macOS (Darwin) Full x86_64 macOS (Darwin) Partial x86_64 Linux Partial WASM32 Partial x86_64 Windows Planned

gofra --help

For full instructions, see Installation.

docs.title: Explanation
docs.text:
This section explains how Gofra works and why — the design decisions behind the language and the compiler. It is not about using Gofra, but about understanding it.

Use it when you want to know why something behaves the way it does, or how a part of the toolchain fits together.

docs.title: Language design
docs.text: Why Gofra is postfix, why it has no unsigned integers, why char is signed, why function values are pointers and not functions, why something is not supported yet. These pages explain the reasoning behind the language.

docs.title: Compiler internals
docs.text: How the type checker works (a type-stack machine), how the optimizer decides what to inline, how modules are compiled and linked. These pages explain the pipeline from source to binary.

docs.title: Module system
docs.text:
Work in progress

The module system is incomplete — both the implementation and this documentation. Use at your own risk.

Gofra has two ways to inject code from other files:

  • #include — the C/C++ preprocessor way. See Reference: preprocessor.
  • import — the module system. This page.

The module system is enabled with the FEATURE_ALLOW_MODULES flag in libgofra.

docs.title: What is a module
docs.text:
A module is a single .gof file, compiled separately into its own object file. The root module is the one passed to gofra.

Example:

// a.gof — root module
import b

func void main[]
    call b.hello_world
end

// b.gof — dependency
#include "std"

pub func void hello_world[]
    "Hello, World!" call println
end

Compiling a.gof:

  1. The compiler parses a.gof and finds import b.
  2. It locates and compiles b.gof into b.o.
  3. It compiles a.gof into a.o, resolving b.hello_world against b.o.
  4. It links a.o and b.o into a.

docs.title: Import syntax
docs.text:
import a                  // a.gof as `a`
import a as my_module     // a.gof as `my_module`
import "my_file.gof" as m // my_file.gof as `m`

docs.title: Visibility
docs.text:
By default, all symbols are private. Mark exposed symbols with pub:

Visibility Meaning pub Available in the module and its dependants private (default) Available only within the module

Calling a private symbol from another module is a compile error.

docs.title: Search order
docs.text:
Module search follows the same rules as #include:

  1. The directory of the current file.
  2. The toolchain's working directory.
  3. Include paths (-isd / --include-search-dir).

docs.title: Dependency order
docs.text:
Dependencies are resolved from source order. A DAG topological sort is applied before codegen:

a -> b -+-> c
        |
        +-> d

Dependencies are compiled first, then the root module.

docs.title: Type checking and optimization
docs.text:
Every module is type-checked independently. Each function symbol is re-checked on compilation.

The optimizer runs in two phases:

  1. Dependencies first, in topological order.
  2. Root module last, over already-optimized dependencies.

This lets the root module apply expensive, high-level optimizations over dependencies without re-optimizing them.

docs.title: Toolchain (compiler) architecture
docs.text: This page describes the internal structure of the Gofra compiler. It is intended for contributors and advanced users.

docs.title: Components
docs.text:
The toolchain consists of:

Component Role CLI Parses arguments, drives the pipeline Lexer Source text → tokens Preprocessor Resolves #-directives on tokens Parser Tokens → HIR Type checker Validates HIR types Optimizer HIR passes Code generator HIR → assembly Assembler Assembly → object file Linker Object files → binary

docs.title: Pipeline
docs.text:
CLI
 → Lexer
 → Preprocessor
 → Parser
 → Optimizer
 → Type checker
 → Code generator
 → Assembler
 → Linker

docs.title: Code generation
docs.text:
By default, all architectures emit assembly (near-machine code). The assembler turns it into binary machine code.

This two-step design has a few advantages:

  • The code generator is simpler — it emits text, not bytes.
  • The assembly can be inspected and debugged.
  • The assembler handles encoding, relocation, and platform-specific details.

docs.title: HIR and type checking
docs.text: The parser produces an HIR (High-level IR) and performs minimal type checking. A separate type checker module validates that types are compatible within operations (arithmetic, function calls, etc.).

docs.title: Intermediate representations
docs.text: IR Produced by Consumed by Tokens Lexer Preprocessor, Parser HIR Parser Type checker, Optimizer, Codegen

docs.title: Optimizer and optimizations
docs.text:
Gofra has a built-in optimizer that runs from top-level HIR passes down to low-level LIR passes, according to the selected target.

This page explains how the optimizer works and why it makes the choices it does. For the list of flags and levels, see the reference.

docs.title: Why the optimizer is off by default
docs.text:
Optimizations are disabled by default (-O0). This is a deliberate choice:

  • Faster builds. Every pass costs time, and a compiler is run many times during development.
  • Easier debugging. Unoptimized code maps more directly to source. Stack traces, breakpoints, and stepping behave predictably.
  • Predictable codegen. When you are debugging the compiler itself, you want to see what the frontend produced, not what the optimizer rewrote it into.

Optimizations are opt-in: -O1.

docs.title: DCE — Dead Code Elimination
docs.text: DCE removes functions that are never called. The motivation is simple: most of a binary's size comes from libraries, and most library functions are never used by a given program. Removing them shrinks the output significantly.

docs.title: Why pub functions are kept
docs.text: A pub function is part of the module's public interface. It may be called from outside the current program — by another module, by an FFI consumer, or by a linker. The optimizer cannot see those callers, so it must assume the function is used.

docs.title: Why DCE iterates
docs.text:
Removing one function may make others unused. If a calls b, and a is removed, b may now be unused too. DCE repeats until no more functions are removed.

This is a fixed-point iteration. The limit (--dce-max-iterations) exists to bound compile time in pathological cases. In practice, 128 iterations is more than enough — most programs converge in a handful.

docs.title: Function inlining
docs.text: Inlining replaces a call with the function body. The motivation is performance: it removes call overhead and exposes the body to further optimization (constant folding, DCE of unused branches, etc.).

docs.title: Why only small functions
docs.text:
Inlining every function would explode binary size. The optimizer uses a heuristic: functions with more operators than --inline-functions-max-operators are not inlined. The threshold trades code size for speed.

A very high threshold inlines almost everything — useful for benchmarks, bad for production binaries.

docs.title: Why recursion is skipped
docs.text:
Inlining a recursive function does not terminate. Consider:

func int fact[int n]
    n 1 <= if
        1 return
    end
    n n 1 - fact * return
end

Inlining fact into itself produces another fact call, which would be inlined again, forever.

The optimizer detects recursion and skips it. This is why inlining is a partial transformation: some calls remain calls.

docs.title: Why iterations matter
docs.text:
Inlining one function may expose new inlineable calls (a function that was called once is now called from an inlined body). The optimizer re-scans until no new inlineable calls appear, bounded by --inline-functions-max-iterations.

If the limit is too low, some inline references are left unresolved. At the assembler stage, these surface as unknown calls — the symbol is marked inline, but the body was never substituted. The fix is to raise the limit; the cost is a slightly larger binary.

docs.title: Type checker
docs.text:
Type checking is always performed at compile time. It validates stack usage and function calls.

This page explains how the type checker works. For the typecast operator, see Reference: type casting

docs.title: Type-stack machine
docs.text:
The type checker is a type-stack machine: it behaves like a stack machine, but operates on types instead of values.

For example, the literal 2 resolves to:

typestack = [int]

Pushing 2 pushes int onto the type stack. Applying + pops two ints and pushes one int.

docs.title: Coverage
docs.text:
The type checker visits every function, including unused ones. A function that is never called is still checked — its body must type-check.

The exception is function calls: an unused function has no calls to check against its signature.

DCE before type checking

If DCE is enabled, it runs before the type checker. Functions removed by DCE are not type-checked.

docs.title: Function checking
docs.text:
For each function, the type checker:

  1. Starts with an empty type stack.
  2. Pushes parameter types as they are consumed.
  3. Validates each operation against the stack.
  4. Checks the return type against the function signature.

When a call is found, the type checker:

  1. Pops the parameter types from the type stack.
  2. Pushes the return type, unless it is void.

docs.title: How-to guides
docs.text:
This section contains recipes for common tasks with Gofra. Each guide answers a specific question: how do I do X?

Use it when you already know the language and want to accomplish something concrete.

docs.title: Install Gofra from source
docs.text: This guide shows how to install Gofra for development.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• Python 3.12 or newer.
  • Poetry.

docs.title: 1. Clone
docs.text:
git clone https://github.com/gofralang/gofra.git
cd gofra

docs.title: 2. Install dependencies
docs.text:
poetry install --with dev

This also installs Ruff:

ruff check .

docs.title: 3. Verify
docs.text:
python -m gofra version

Local gofra

Inside the Poetry environment (poetry shell), the local gofra command shadows the system-wide one.

docs.title: Call C functions from Gofra
docs.text:
This guide shows how to call functions from a C library in Gofra.

For background on FFI, see Wikipedia. For the extern attribute, see Reference: attributes.

docs.title: Declare the external function
docs.text:
Mark the function with extern and give it a Gofra type contract:

extern func int puts[*char[] s]

This matches the C declaration:

int puts(const char *s);

extern functions cannot have a body — only a signature.

docs.title: Link the library
docs.text:
Tell the linker which library to link against with -l:

gofra build hello.gof -lraylib

If the library is not found by pkg-config, add a search directory with -L:

gofra build hello.gof -lraylib -L/opt/homebrew/lib --no-pkg-config

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
extern func int puts[*char[] s]

func void main[]
    "Hello, World!" puts drop
end

gofra build hello.gof -lc

puts is called with a C-string; its return value is dropped.

docs.title: No variadic arguments
docs.text: Gofra does not support calling variadic C functions (printf, etc.) directly. The workaround is to write a non-variadic wrapper in C and call that:

docs.title: Calling convention
docs.text: extern functions use the C calling convention. Gofra functions use the Gofra calling convention. They are not interchangeable.

docs.title: Install Gofra
docs.text: This guide shows how to install the Gofra toolchain with pip.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• Python 3.12 or newer.

For native targets: linker (ld) and assembler (as). For WASM: wat2wasm from WABT.

docs.title: Install
docs.text: pip install gofra

docs.title: Verify
docs.text: gofra version

docs.title: Compile and run for WebAssembly
docs.text:
This guide shows how to compile a Gofra program to WebAssembly and run it in a WASM runtime.

For background on WASM, see wasm.org

docs.title: Compile to WASM
docs.text:
Use --target wasm (or -t wasm):

gofra build hello_world.gof -t wasm -of object

This emits hello_world.wasm.

-of object is required

The WASM target does not support -of executable: WASM is not an executable format on its own. It must be loaded by a runtime.

docs.title: Run the artifact
docs.text:
A .wasm file needs a loader. The compiler repository includes a Node.js loader:

examples/wasm/node_example_loader.js

Run it with:

node examples/wasm/node_example_loader.js hello_world.wasm

Browser

The same loader logic works in a browser with minor changes to how the .wasm file is fetched. See examples/wasm/example_wasm_raylib_layer_loader.html for a browser example with graphics.

docs.title: Reference
docs.text:
This section is the complete reference for the Gofra language. It documents syntax, semantics, and rules — not tutorials or explanations.

Use it when you need to look up an exact detail: a keyword's syntax, a type's size, an attribute's effect, a cast rule.

Pages are written to be read out of order. Every page is self-contained and links to its dependencies.

docs.title: Attributes
docs.text: Attribute in Gofra is an keyword that is applied to object (function, variable, type)

docs.title: pub
docs.text:
Applies to: functions

Mark function as exposed to other modules, and exposed inside compiled object file as function symbol for later linking

Example for module system:

// mod.gof:
pub func f[]
end

// When importing module with this function, it allows to call and use that function in any way:

import mod;
call mod.f

Example for object file linkage:

pub func f[]
end

// When compiling down to object file,
// symbol `f` remains public, and you can link that object file with other objects that externs `f` at linkage

docs.title: naked
docs.text:
Applies to: functions

Naked functions does not have prologue and epilogue in machine code nor any compiled inserted code, they contains only assembly instructions.

They allows to write functions which will be broken due to compiler inserted code

For example:

naked func void f[]
    // no prologue
    inline_raw_asm "{machine_instructions}"
    inline_raw_asm "ret"
    // no epilogue
end

Notice: as compiler cannot insert boilerplate instructions into these functions, you must comply with return logic (link-registers) and manage arguments by own, naked functions supports parameters but it is only for type checking and calling convention only

docs.title: extern
docs.text:
Applies to: functions

Mark function as defined somewhere else and not in produced artifact (object file, executable), for later linking with library/object file.

Those functions cannot have any body/operators inside it.

For example external function puts from libc library is declared as:

extern func int _puts[*char[]]

Compiler will try its best to perform such call assuming Gofra/C call convention / ABI

Read more about FFI...

docs.title: inline
docs.text:
Applies to: functions

Functions that marked as inline has no real call, it unwraps its body directly from direct call (inside caller)

Compiler tries to apply these attributes to inlineable functions via heuristics while inline optimizations are enabled

For example:

func int f[]
    32 return
end

// On non inline call:
f return // yields 32

// If there is `inline` attribute
32 return // yields 32, expanded from inline function

Read more about optimizations...

docs.title: no_return
docs.text:
Applies to: functions

Mark function as having no possible way out, for example exit system function, these function must has no return value

Compiler will warn you if you have function that always calls to no_return functions Attribute allows to emit general compiler warnings and errors and perform possible optimizations, mostly used in compiler library, but useful if you calling exit function and has nothing more

This checks ran only at compile-time and has no effect on runtime

no_return func void x[]
    // Must has no way out
end

func void x1[]
   call exit // warning, always calling to `no_return` function - propagate attribute

   2 2 + drop // warning, unreachable code, and allows to apply optimizations like DCE
end

func void x1[]
    false if ==
        call exit // may have conditional `no_return` calls without any warning
    end
end

docs.title: reorder
docs.text:
Applies to: structures

Apply reordering to structure. Reordering is a process when for performance reasons, fields of structure being re-ordered to solve alignment issues (redundant padding on structure memory layout)

By default, structures does not apply reordering, overridde by specifying this attribute.

Compiler will warn you if you have possible reordering on any structure

struct bad_layout
    a char // 1 byte
    b int  // 8 byte
    c char // 1 byte
end // Unpacked, 24 bytes

struct reorder reordered_layout
    a char // 1 byte
    b int  // 8 byte
    c char // 1 byte
end // Unpacked, reordered 16 bytes
// Order was transformed into [b, a, c] (int, char, char) re-using padding from int to char

docs.title: packed
docs.text:
Applies to: structures

Apply packing to structure. Packing is a process when compiler removes all padding between fields of structure, laying them out contiguously in memory without any alignment.

By default, structures are padded to satisfy alignment requirements of their fields. Override by specifying this attribute.

Compiler will warn you if you have possible packing on any structure

struct unpacked_layout
    a char // 1 byte
    b int  // 8 byte, aligned to 8 bytes -> 7 bytes padding before
    c char // 1 byte
end // Padded, 24 bytes

struct packed packed_layout
    a char // 1 byte
    b int  // 8 byte, no padding before
    c char // 1 byte
end // Packed, 10 bytes
// Layout is [a, b, c] with no padding between fields

docs.title: Command-line interface
docs.text:
The gofra command is the entry point to the toolchain.

gofra <command> [options]

docs.text: Command Description version Show version targets List available targets run Compile and run a source file clean Clean build cache and artifacts build Compile a source file

docs.title: gofra build
docs.text:
Compile a Gofra source file into an executable, object, or library.

gofra build [options] <source_file>

docs.title: Control flow
docs.text: Gofra provides conditional execution and looping constructs.

docs.title: if
docs.text: Executes a block if the condition is true.

docs.title: Syntax
docs.text:
<condition> if
    <body>
end

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
1 1 == if
    "true" print
end

docs.title: else
docs.text:
<condition> if
    <then>
else
    <else>
end

1 0 == if
    "equal" print
else
    "not equal" print
end

docs.title: while
docs.text: Repeats a block while the condition is true.

docs.title: Syntax
docs.text:
while
    <condition>
do
    <body>
end

The condition is evaluated before each iteration.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
var counter int = 0

while
    counter 10 <
do
    counter print_integer
    &counter counter 1 + !<
end

docs.title: for
docs.text: Iterates over a range or a array. Ranges are exclusive on the upper bound.

docs.title: Range iteration
docs.text:
for i in 0..10 do
    // i = 0, 1, 2, ..., 9
end

Reversed ranges count down:

for i in 10..0 do
    // i = 9, 8, ..., 0
end

docs.title: Variable bounds
docs.text:
var x = 5

for i in 0..x do
    // i = 0, 1, 2, 3, 4
end

Step is always 1

for ranges always step by 1 (or −1 for reversed ranges). There is no custom step.

docs.title: Iterating arrays
docs.text:
var xs = [5, 6, 7]

for i in 0..xs do
    // i = 0, 1, 2 (index)
end

for x in xs do
    // x = *5, *6, *7 (pointer to each element)
end

Pointer iteration

for x in xs iterates by pointer: x is a pointer to the current element, not a copy of its value.

docs.title: Lowering
docs.text:
for i in 0..10 is lowered to:

var i int = 0
while
    i 10 <
do
    <body>
    &i i 1 + !<
end

For a reversed range (10..0), the comparison is > and the increment is -.

docs.title: Functions
docs.text: A function is a named block of code with parameters and a return type.

docs.title: Syntax
docs.text:
func <return-type> <name>[<params>]
    <body>
end

Parameters are written as <type> <name>, separated by commas:

func i64 add[i64 a, i64 b]
    a b + return
end

docs.title: Return type
docs.text:
The return type follows func:

func void f[]        // returns nothing
func int f[]         // returns int
func *char[] f[]     // returns a C-string pointer

A void function cannot return a value:

func void f[]
    32 return    // error: void function returns a value
end

A non-void function must return a value:

func int f[]
    // error: missing return
end

docs.title: Calling
docs.text:
A function is called by pushing its arguments onto the stack and then calling it:

2 3 add

call is optional

call f and f are equivalent for direct calls. The call keyword is required only when calling through a function pointer variable or using modules:

call v      // v is a function pointer variable
call mod.v  // v is a member of `mod` module

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text:
Arguments are passed on the stack, in order. The function pops them according to its signature into parameter variables.

func i64 add[i64 a, i64 b]
    a b + return
end

2 3 add    // 5

docs.title: void functions
docs.text:
A void function produces no value:

func void print_hello[]
    "hello" print
end

call print_hello

docs.title: extern functions
docs.text:
An extern function is declared but not defined in the current compilation unit. It is resolved at link time:

extern func int puts[*char[]]

extern functions have no body.

See extern for details.

docs.title: pub functions
docs.text:
A pub function is exported from the module and emitted as a public symbol:

pub func f[]
    // ...
end

See pub for details.

docs.title: Recursion
docs.text:
Functions may call themselves:

func i64 fact[i64 n]
    n 1 <= if
        1 return
    end
    n n 1 - fact * return
end

docs.title: Keywords
docs.text: Reserved words in Gofra. They cannot be used as identifiers.

docs.title: Declarations
docs.text: Keyword Description func function declaration var variable declaration const constant declaration struct structure declaration union union declaration type type alias / generic definition import module import

docs.title: Attributes
docs.text:

docs.title: Lambdas
docs.text: A lambda is an anonymous function defined inline. It produces a function pointer.

docs.title: Syntax
docs.text:
lambda func <ret> _[<params>]
    <body>
end

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
type F_T func int _[int, int]

func F_T make_adder[]
    lambda func int _[int, int]
        + return
    end
    return
end

The lambda produces a function pointer of type func int _[int, int].

docs.title: No captures
docs.text:
A lambda cannot capture variables from the enclosing function:

func F_T make_adder[int n]
    lambda func int _[int]
        n + return    // error: `n` is not captured
    end
    return
end

docs.title: Literals
docs.text:
A literal is a value written directly in source code. In Gofra's postfix syntax, a literal pushes its value onto the stack.

42          // pushes 42
0x4124      // pushes 16676
-17         // pushes -17
"hello"     // pushes a string (*string)
'a'         // pushes a char
true        // pushes a bool

docs.title: Integer literals
docs.text:
Integer literals are written in decimal or hexadecimal:

42
0
-17
0x4124
0xFF

Type: int (8 bytes, signed).

Negative literals

-17 is a single integer literal, not the unary minus applied to 17. The sign is part of the literal.

Hexadecimal

0x4124 is the same value as 16676 in decimal.

docs.title: Character literals
docs.text:
Character literals use single quotes:

'a'
'Z'
'\n'
'\0'
'\x41'

docs.title: String literals
docs.text:
String literals use double quotes:

"hello"
""
"Hello, World\n"

Type: *string. See string for details.

docs.title: Boolean literals
docs.text:
true
false

docs.title: Operators
docs.text: Gofra operators are postfix: they follow their operands.

docs.title: Arithmetic
docs.text:
Operator Mnemonic Description + a b -> c addition - a b -> c subtraction * a b -> c multiplication / a b -> c division % a b -> c modulo 
2 3 +    // 5
10 3 %   // 1

docs.title: Comparison
docs.text: Operator Mnemonic Description == a b -> bool equal != a b -> bool not equal < a b -> bool less than > a b -> bool greater than <= a b -> bool less or equal >= a b -> bool greater or equal

docs.title: Logical
docs.text: Operator Mnemonic Description && bool bool -> bool AND \|\| bool bool -> bool OR lnot bool -> bool NOT

docs.title: Bitwise
docs.text:
Operator Mnemonic Description & a b -> c AND \| a b -> c OR ^ a b -> c XOR << a b -> c shift left >> a b -> c shift right 
2 3 <<    // 16
2 3 >>    // 0
2 3 &     // 2
2 3 ^     // 1

docs.title: Memory
docs.text:
Operator Mnemonic Description !< addr val -> _ _ store val at addr ?> addr -> val load from addr 
var x int
&x 10 !<    // x = 10
&x ?>       // 10

docs.title: Preprocessor
docs.text:
The preprocessor is a compilation stage that operates on lexer tokens, before the parser. It resolves #-directives and macro references.

All preprocessor directives begin with #.

docs.title: #include
docs.text:
#include inserts the contents of another file at the point of the directive.

#include "sum.gof"

func void main[]
    2 2 sum    // `sum` is defined in sum.gof
end

Inclusion is recursive: definitions from the included file are available at the include site, and the included file may itself #include other files.

docs.title: Module include
docs.text:
Including a directory includes the file with the same name inside it:

#include "dir"    // includes `dir/dir.gof`

This simplifies library layout: a library foo is a directory foo/ with foo/foo.gof as its entry point.

Include-once

Each file is included at most once per compilation, even if it is #included from multiple places.

docs.title: Search strategy
docs.text:
When resolving #include, Gofra searches in this order:

  1. The directory of the including file.
  2. The directory of the main file.
  3. Include search directories (-isd / --include-search-dir).

docs.title: #define and #undef
docs.text:
#define creates a macro. #undef removes it.

#define MACRO 2

The macro can be used anywhere in the code after its definition:

MACRO MACRO +    // 2 2 + = 4

docs.title: From the command line
docs.text:
Macros can be defined from the CLI with -D:

gofra build -Ddebug=1 main.gof

This is useful for debug flags and feature toggles.

docs.title: #ifdef, #ifndef, #endif
docs.text:
Conditional compilation based on macro definition:

#ifdef DEBUG
    // compiled only if DEBUG is defined
#endif

#ifndef DEBUG
    // compiled only if DEBUG is not defined
#endif

docs.title: Built-in macros
docs.text:
Gofra defines two macros for the target:

Macro Example Meaning OS_{NAME} OS_LINUX, OS_DARWIN Target operating system ARCH_{NAME} ARCH_AMD64, ARCH_AARCH64 Target architecture IS_{ENDIANNES}_ENDIAN IS_LITTLE_ENDIAN, IS_BIG_ENDIAN ...

For example, compiling for Darwin on ARM64 defines OS_DARWIN and ARCH_AARCH64.

docs.title: Variables
docs.text: A variable is a named container for a value of a specific type. Variables can be local (inside a function) or global (at top level).

docs.title: Declaration
docs.text:
var <name> <type>

Examples:

var x int
var c char
var p *int
var a int[32]

The type is required unless an initializer allows inference (see below).

docs.title: Initializers
docs.text:
A variable can be initialized at declaration:

var x int = 10
var c char = 'a'
var s *string = "Hello, World"
var a int[3] = [1, 2, 3]

docs.title: Type inference
docs.text:
If the initializer determines the type unambiguously, the type may be omitted:

var x = 5                  // int
var s = "test"             // *string
var a = [1, 2, 3]          // int[3]
var a int[] = [1, 2, 3]    // int[3], unfinished -> finished declaration

Ambiguous initializers require an explicit type:

var e = []    // error: cannot infer element type

docs.title: Constants
docs.text:
A variable with a compile-time known initializer can be declared const:

const x = 5
const y int = 10

A constant:

  • Cannot be modified after declaration.
  • Cannot have its address taken (&x is an error).
  • May be inlined and eliminated by the optimizer.
const x = 5

&x         // error: cannot take address of a constant

docs.title: Storage duration
docs.text:
The storage duration of a variable depends on where it is declared:

Where Storage Initialization Top level Global (static segment) Zero-initialized Inside a function Local (stack) Uninitialized unless initialized at declaration 
var global int    // zero-initialized

func void main[]
    var local int    // uninitialized
end

docs.title: Optimizations
docs.text: Gofra's optimizer applies the following passes. Each pass has a minimum optimization level and can be toggled individually.

docs.title: Levels
docs.text: Level Passes -O0 none (default) -O1 DCE, function inlining -O2 -O1 + additional passes

docs.title: Passes
docs.text: Pass Min level Flag Impact DCE -O1 -fdce / -fno-dce Reduced binary size Function inlining -O1 -finline-functions / -fno-inline-functions Increased size, increased performance

docs.title: Targets
docs.text:
List all current compilation targets via gofra targets

Gofra compiles to the following targets:

Target Architecture OS Status amd64-apple-darwin x86_64 MacOS stable arm64-apple-darwin ARM64 MacOS experimental amd64-unknown-linux x86_64 Linux experimental amd64-unknown-windows x86_64 Windows experimental wasm32-unknown-none WASM32 - experimental

docs.title: Array types
docs.text: An array is a contiguous, fixed-size block of elements of the same type. The size is part of the type and cannot change after declaration.

docs.title: Syntax
docs.text:
The array type is written as the element type followed by square brackets:

int[32]    // array of 32 integers
char[256]  // array of 256 chars
int[]      // incomplete array (see below)

docs.title: Layout
docs.text:
An array is a contiguous block of memory. The array value points to the first element; subsequent elements follow at byte offsets scaled by the element size.

//  [element0][element1][element2]
//   ^
// array

For int (8 bytes), int[3] is laid out as:

Index Offset (bytes) 0 0 1 8 2 16

Byte-scaled pointer arithmetic

Gofra pointer arithmetic is byte-scaled, not element-scaled. To reach element i of int[N], add i 8 * (i sizeof int *) bytes — not i. The [] operator does this scaling automatically.

docs.title: Initialization
docs.text:
Initialization depends on storage duration:

Storage Initialization Global / static Zero-initialized Stack (local) Uninitialized — reading before writing is UB

"Uninitialized stack arrays"

Stack arrays are not zero-initialized. The contents are whatever was on the stack before. Always initialize before reading.

docs.title: List initializer
docs.text:
An array can be initialized with a list of values:

var a int[3] = [1, 2, 3]

The array size must match the number of values:

var a int[3] = [1, 2, 3]    // OK
var b int[2] = [1, 2, 3]    // error: too many values
var c int[4] = [1, 2, 3]    // error: too few values

docs.title: Filler
docs.text:
To fill the remaining elements with a value, use ; followed by the filler:

var a int[5] = [1, 2, 3; 0]    // [1, 2, 3, 0, 0]

The filler applies to all elements after the explicitly listed ones.

docs.title: Manual initialization
docs.text:
For other types, or to set values conditionally, write to elements directly:

var a int[3]
&a[0] 10 !<
&a[1] 20 !<
&a[2] 30 !<

After this, all three elements are initialized and safe to read.

docs.title: Accessing elements
docs.text:
The [] operator computes the address of the element at the given index:

var a int[32]

a[0]    // int — first element
a[3]    // int — fourth element

The index can be a constant or a variable:

var i int = 3
a[i]    // int — element at index `i`

docs.title: Pointer arithmetic equivalent
docs.text:
a[i] is equivalent to:

a 8 i * +    // a + (8 * i) — for int (8 bytes)

docs.title: Bounds checking
docs.text:
Gofra performs compile-time bounds checking where the index is a constant:

var a int[5]
a[5]    // compile error: index out of bounds for `int[5]`

Runtime bounds are not checked

When the index is a runtime value, Gofra does not check bounds. Accessing out-of-bounds memory is undefined behavior (segfault).

This can be overriden via experimental flag: --rt-bounds-checks/--oob-checks

docs.title: Incomplete arrays
docs.text:
An incomplete array type is written T[] — with no size. It cannot be used as a variable or field type:

var x int[]    // error: incomplete array type

It is used as a function parameter type, meaning "an array of any size":

func void process[*int[]]
    // ...
end

The function accepts *int[N] for any N:

var a int[32]
var b int[1]

&a call process    // OK
&b call process    // OK

No size information

An incomplete array parameter does not carry its length. If the function needs the size, pass it as a separate parameter.

docs.title: bool type
docs.text: A bool is a boolean type with two values: true and false. It is used for conditions, logical operations, and flags.

docs.title: Size and alignment
docs.text: Type Size Alignment Values bool 1 byte 1 true, false

docs.title: Representation
docs.text:
Internally, a bool is an integer:

Value Byte false 0 true 1

"Invariant"

A well-formed bool is always 0 or 1. Other byte values are not valid bool values, but can appear after a REINTERPRET cast from an integer.

docs.title: lnot (Logical NOT)
docs.text:
true lnot    // false
false lnot   // true

docs.title: && (Logical AND)
docs.text:
true true &&    // true
true false &&   // false
false false &&  // false

docs.title: || (Logical OR)
docs.text:
true false ||   // true
false false ||  // false

docs.title: To bool
docs.text:
An integer can be cast to bool with NORMALIZE_BOOL: non-zero becomes true, zero becomes false.

0 typecast bool    // false
42 typecast bool   // true

docs.title: From bool
docs.text:
A bool can be cast to an integer. The value extends to the integer type.

true typecast i64    // 1
false typecast i64   // 0

docs.title: char type
docs.text: A char is a single-byte character type.

docs.title: Size and alignment
docs.text: Type Size Alignment Range char 1 byte 1 −128 .. 127

docs.title: Relationship to i8
docs.text:
char and i8 are both 1 byte, but they are distinct types. Converting between them requires an explicit typecast:

'a' typecast i8    // 97
97 typecast char   // 'a'

The cast is REINTERPRET — the byte is not modified.

docs.title: Literals
docs.text:
Character literals use single quotes:

// push char code on the stack
'a'
'Z'
'0'
' '

docs.title: Functions and function pointers
docs.text: In Gofra, functions can be referenced through function pointers. A function pointer is a first-class value: it can be assigned to variables, passed as arguments, and called.

docs.title: Function type
docs.text:
A function type is written func <ret> _[<params>]. The _ is a placeholder for the function name — otherwise name will be dropped, so it is useless.

func void _[]           // () -> void
func i64 _[i64, i64]    // (i64, i64) -> i64

docs.title: Type aliases
docs.text:
Use type to give a function type a name:

type FunctionType func void _[]

var x FunctionType;
var v func void _[];    // same type, written inline

docs.title: Getting a function pointer
docs.text:
pointer_of_proc pushes a pointer to the given function onto the stack:

func void f[]
    // ...
end

pointer_of_proc f    // *func void _[]

docs.title: Calling a function through a pointer
docs.text:
To call a function through a variable, use call:

func void f[]
    // ...
end

func void main[]
    var v func void _[];

    &v pointer_of_proc f !<

    call v
end

docs.title: Integer types
docs.text:
Gofra has fixed-size signed integer types. All integer types are primitive: they have a known size in bytes and a known alignment, both equal to the size.

No unsigned types

There are no unsigned integer types (u8, u16, u32, u64). All integer types are signed.

docs.title: Size and alignment
docs.text: Type Size Alignment Range i8 1 byte 1 −128 .. 127 i16 2 bytes 2 −32 768 .. 32 767 i32 4 bytes 4 −2 147 483 648 .. 2 147 483 647 i64 8 bytes 8 −2^63 .. 2^63 − 1

docs.title: int alias
docs.text:
int is a language-level alias for i64. It is the canonical integer type used throughout the standard library and in examples.

var x int   // same as `var x i64`, 8 bytes
var y i64   // explicit 64-bit
var z i32   // 32-bit
var w i8    // 8-bit

int is not architecture dependant

int is always 64-bit on every target. It does not depend on the pointer width or on the target architecture.

docs.title: Arithmetic
docs.text: Integer types support the arithmetic operators +, -, *, /, %.

docs.title: Pointer types
docs.text:
A pointer holds the memory address of another value. Pointer types are written *T, where T is the pointee type.

*i8       // pointer to i8
*i64      // pointer to i64
*char[]   // pointer to a char array (C-string)
*MyStruct // pointer to MyStruct

docs.title: Size and alignment
docs.text:
Type Size (64-bit) Alignment *T 8 bytes 8

Always 64bit archicture

Compiler supports only 64 bit architectures assumes pointers are always 64 bit

docs.title: Address-of
docs.text:
The & operator takes the address of an lvalue:

var x i64 = 120
&x                // *i64

Nested fields:

struct Point
    x i64
    y i64
end

var p Point
&p.x              // *i64

docs.title: Dereference
docs.text:
There is no auto-dereference of pointers for raw value, rather you can use this syntax:

var x *i64;

x ?> // read

docs.title: Between pointers
docs.text:
Any pointer can be cast to any other pointer with REINTERPRET:

var x i64 = 120
&x typecast *i8   // *i64 -> *i8

docs.title: Pointer <-> integer
docs.text:
An integer can be cast to a pointer and back, provided the integer size matches the pointer size:

&x typecast i64   // *i64 -> i64 (64-bit target)
120 typecast *i8  // i64 -> *i8

docs.title: string type
docs.text:
Strings in Gofra are represented as fat pointers — also known as string views or string slices.

A string is a pair of:

  • a pointer to the underlying bytes (*char[]),
  • a length in bytes (int).

The data itself is not owned by the string value — it lives elsewhere (typically in a read-only static data segment).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
//"Declaration"
var s string = "Hello"

"another text" // *string

s.data   // *char[] — pointer to bytes
s.len    // 5 — byte length

// Passing around
func get_len[*string s]
    s.len
end

&s print_len // 5
"test" get_len // 4

docs.title: Fields
docs.text: Field Type Description .data *char[] Pointer to the underlying C-string bytes .len int Length in bytes (not characters)

docs.title: .data
docs.text: Underlying pointer to the C-string (*char[]).

docs.title: .len
docs.text: Size of the string in bytes.

docs.title: Internal representation
docs.text:
The string type is a structure available to every compiled program. It is defined as:

struct string
    data *char[]
    len int
end

docs.title: Storage
docs.text:
String literals are stored in the static data segment of the compiled binary and must have read-only memory protection.

This means:

  • The bytes are not copied when a string value is passed around.
  • A string value does not own its data.
  • Modifying the underlying bytes is undefined behavior.

docs.title: Structures
docs.text: A struct is a composite type with named fields of possibly different types. Fields are laid out contiguously in memory, with padding inserted to satisfy each field's alignment.

docs.title: Syntax
docs.text:
struct <Name>
    <field> <Type>
    <field> <Type>
    ...
end

docs.title: Declaration
docs.text:
struct Person
    age int
    name *char[]
end

docs.title: Field access
docs.text:
Fields are accessed with . (dot). The expression pushes the address of the field, so it can be used as an lvalue for both reading and writing.

var stepan Person

stepan.age        // int — value of `age`
&stepan.age        // *int — address of `age`

a.b.c.d // Also possible

docs.title: Memory layout
docs.text:
Fields are laid out in declaration order, with padding inserted to satisfy each field's alignment. The total size is rounded up to the struct's alignment.

struct BadLayout
    a char   // offset 0,  size 1
    b int    // offset 8,  size 8 (7 bytes padding before)
    c char   // offset 16, size 1
end
// sizeof = 24, align = 8

Layout diagram:

Packed (tight):
|a|    b   |c|          => 10 bytes

Aligned:
|a|...padding...|    b    |...padding...|c|   => 24 bytes

Padding is inserted on both sides of b to align the 8-byte int field.

docs.title: packed
docs.text:
Removes all padding between fields:

struct packed Tight
    a char
    b int
    c char
end
// sizeof = 10

docs.title: reorder
docs.text:
Reorders fields to eliminate padding, keeping alignment:

struct reorder Reordered
    a char
    b int
    c char
end
// Reordered to [b, a, c], sizeof = 16

See packed and reorder for details.

docs.title: Self-reference
docs.text:
A struct can contain a reference to itself or itself:

struct Node
    value int
    next *Node
end

docs.title: offset_of
docs.text:
Pushes the byte offset of a field within a struct:

offset_of <Struct> <field>

struct Foo
    a int
    b int
end

offset_of Foo a   // 0
offset_of Foo b   // 8

Takes alignment and reordering into account. The result matches the ABI used in generated machine code.

docs.title: align_of
docs.text:
Pushes the alignment of a type:

align_of <Type>

align_of Foo        // 8
align_of int        // 8
align_of char       // 1
align_of int[32]    // 8 — alignment of `int`

docs.title: Generic structures
docs.text:
A struct can be parameterized by a type:

struct Generic{T}
    field_a T
    field_b T
    field_c int
end

var x Generic{T = int}

docs.title: Union types
docs.text:
A union is an overlapping type: all of its members share the same memory. Its size is the maximum of all its members' sizes, rounded up to the largest alignment requirement.

Only one member is meaningful at a time. Writing to one member invalidates the others.

docs.title: Syntax
docs.text:
union <Name>
    <field> <Type>
    <field> <Type>
    ...
end

docs.title: Declaration
docs.text:
union MyUnion
    as_2b i16
    as_8b i64
end

docs.title: Size
docs.text:
The size of a union is the size of its largest member:

union MyUnion
    as_2b i16   // 2 bytes
    as_8b i64   // 8 bytes
end
// sizeof MyUnion = 8

docs.title: Memory layout
docs.text:
All members start at offset 0 and overlap:

*MyUnion = [ ...8 bytes... ]
             ^
             all members start here

When you access a member, the compiler reads exactly the number of bytes required by that member's type.

union MyUnion
    as_2b i16
    as_8b i64
end

docs.title: Accessing members
docs.text:
Members are accessed with . (dot), same as structures.

struct Foo
    a int
    b int
end

struct Bar
    a char
    b char
    c int
end

union MyUnion
    foo Foo
    bar Bar
end

var x MyUnion;

Writing to a member:

&x.bar.c 10 !<

Reading it back:

x.bar.c

docs.title: Ordering and alignment
docs.text:
Field ordering and alignment do not apply to unions. A union uses a single memory chunk for all variants, so there is nothing to reorder or pad.

As a result:

  • offset_of any member is 0.
  • align_of a union is the maximum alignment over all its members.

docs.title: Attributes
docs.text:
The following attributes cannot be applied to unions:

  • reorder
  • packed

Both are meaningless for a type with overlapping members.

docs.title: "Type punning"
docs.text:
union Bits
    as_int i64
    as_ptr *char[]
end

var b Bits;
42 b.as_int !<
b.as_ptr // *char[]

docs.title: void type
docs.text:
void is the absence of a type. It is used as the return type of functions that produce no value.

Not a value

void has no size, no alignment, and no values. It cannot be stored, passed, or returned. It only marks that a function returns nothing.

docs.title: Function return type
docs.text:
A function with return type void produces no value:

func void f[]
    // ...
end

Calling it leaves nothing on the stack:

call f

docs.title: Untyped pointers
docs.text: var ptr *void; // mark ptr as pointing to *anything*

docs.title: Rules
docs.text:
• void cannot be used as a variable type:
var x void   // error
  • void cannot be used as a struct or union field type:
struct S
    x void   // error
end
  • void cannot be a parameter type:
func f[void]   // error
  • A void function cannot return a value:
func void f[]
    32 return   // error: function returns `void`
end
  • A non-void function must return a value:
func int f[]
    // error: missing return
end

docs.title: Generic types
docs.text: A generic type is a lazy template for a concrete type. It is parameterized by one or more type parameters and is not usable until applied to concrete types.

docs.title: Terminology
docs.text: Term Example Meaning Type parameter T in Identity{T} Placeholder for a type Type argument int in Identity{T = int} Concrete type bound to a parameter Generic type Identity{T} Unapplied template Applied generic Identity{T = int} Concrete type after application Concrete type int, *int, int[3] Fully resolved type with known size

docs.title: Concrete types
docs.text:
A concrete type has a known size in bytes. It can be used as a variable type, a struct field type, or a function parameter type.

Primitive types (int, char, bool, …) are concrete. Composite types over concrete types (*int, int[3], struct Point) are also concrete.

Generic types are not concrete. They cannot be used directly

docs.title: Defining a generic type
docs.text:
A generic type is defined with type and =:

type Identity{T} T
type XT{T} *T
type Array{T, N} T[N]

A generic struct is defined with struct:

struct Slice{T, K}
    data *T[K]
    len int
end

docs.title: Applying a generic type
docs.text:
Applying a generic type to concrete arguments produces a concrete type:

type Identity{T} T

var x Identity{T = int}    // typeof(x) is `int`

With value arguments:

type Array{T, N} T[N]

var arr Array{T = int, N = 3}    // int[3]

Type parameter names are required

Application must name the type parameter: Identity{T = int}, not Identity{int}.

docs.title: Type casting (typecast)
docs.text: Keyword typecast is used for explicit casting type A to type B (value typecast T)

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
120 typecast i8 // i64 (int) -> i8

// Casting pointers
var x i64 = 120;
&x typecast *i8 // *i64 -> *i
?> // Resolves to i8

// Warning: useless typecast
120 typecast i64 // i64 -> i64

// Error: cannot cast type `int` to type `T1`
struct T1 ... end
120 typecast T1  // i64 -> T1

docs.title: Cast types
docs.text: Kind Description REINTERPRET Does not modify the value — only its interpretation TRUNCATE Loses information — target is smaller than source EXTEND Adds information — target is larger than source NORMALIZE_BOOL Compares against zero — non-zero becomes true

docs.title: Cast rules
docs.text:
From To Kind Notes *T *U REINTERPRET Any pointer to any pointer integer *T REINTERPRET Integer size must equal pointer size (e.g. i64 on 64-bit) *T integer REINTERPRET Same constraint as above bool integer REINTERPRET Boolean invariant, extends to integer T T REINTERPRET Both integer or char, same byte size (e.g. i8 → char) T T TRUNCATE Both integer or char, source bigger than target (e.g. i64 → i8) T T EXTEND Both integer or char, target bigger than source (e.g. i8 → i64) integer bool NORMALIZE_BOOL Non-zero → true, zero → false

Casts not listed above are rejected at compile time.

docs.title: REINTERPRET
docs.text:
Does not modifies value, just another interpretation of bytes

  • T -> T (any pointer to any pointer)
  • integer -> *T (treating integer as pointer requires integer size to be same as target architecture pointer size, such on 64bit, integer must be i64, as others has invariant pointer)
  • *T -> integer (same as int -> *T)
  • bool -> integer (therefore, booleans invariants integer, it does extends to integer)
  • T -> T, where both are integer nor char and their byte size is same (i8 -> char)

docs.title: TRUNCATE
docs.text:
Cast with losing information

  • T -> T, where both are integer nor char and source type byte size is bigger (i64 -> i8)

docs.title: EXTEND
docs.text:
Cast without losing information: add additonal bytes

  • T -> T, where both are integer nor char and target type byte size is bigger (i8 -> i64)

docs.title: NORMALIZE_BOOL
docs.text:
Does compares value against zero, true on non-zero value

  • integer -> bool

docs.title: Type definition
docs.text: The type keyword creates an alias for an existing type. An alias can be plain (no parameters) or generic (with type parameters).

docs.title: Syntax
docs.text:
type <Name> <TypeExpr>
type <Name>{<T>, <U>} <TypeExpr>

docs.title: Plain aliases
docs.text:
An alias without type parameters:

type MyInt int
type Callback func void _[]
type IntPtr *int

docs.title: Generic aliases
docs.text:
An alias with type parameters:

type Array{T, N} T[N]
type Pointer{T} *T

docs.title: Rules
docs.text:
• A plain alias is transparent: MyInt and int are the same type at compile time. No runtime cost, no new type.
  • A generic alias is monomorphized: each instantiation produces a separate type.
  • Aliases cannot be used to create distinct types.

docs.title: std/assert
docs.text:
Runtime assertions.

#include "std/assert.gof"

docs.title: runtime_assert
docs.text:
pub func void runtime_assert[int a, int b, *string sv]

Checks that a == b. If not, prints "runtime_assert: Assertion failed, " followed by sv to STD_ERR, then calls abort.

1 1 "values must be equal" call runtime_assert    // passes
1 2 "values must be equal" call runtime_assert    // aborts

docs.title: assert
docs.text:
Alias for runtime_assert:

#define assert runtime_assert

1 1 "values must be equal" call assert

Integers only

runtime_assert compares int values. It cannot compare other types (generics are not supported yet).

Aborts the process

On failure, runtime_assert calls abort. It does not throw or return.

docs.title: std/char
docs.text:
Utilities for working with the char type.

#include "std/char"

docs.title: is_digit
docs.text:
pub func bool is_digit[char c]

Returns true if c is an ASCII digit ('0'..'9').

'5' call is_digit    // true
'a' call is_digit    // false

ASCII only

is_digit checks the ASCII range. It does not recognize Unicode digits.

docs.title: digit_to_int
docs.text:
pub func int digit_to_int[char c]

Converts a digit character to its integer value.

'5' call digit_to_int    // 5
'0' call digit_to_int    // 0

No validation

digit_to_int does not check that c is a digit. Passing a non-digit character returns a meaningless result.

docs.title: std/random
docs.text:
Pseudo-random number generator (PRNG).

#include "std/random"

Xorshift

The PRNG uses the Xorshift algorithm. It is not cryptographically secure.

docs.title: State
docs.text:
The PRNG has a single global state:

var std_prng_random_state int

Global variables are zero-initialized. To get non-deterministic output, seed the state explicitly.

docs.title: set_random_seed
docs.text:
pub func void set_random_seed[int seed]

Sets the PRNG state to seed.

12345 call set_random_seed

docs.title: random
docs.text:
pub func int random[]

Advances the PRNG state and returns the next value.

call random    // some int

docs.title: random_range
docs.text:
pub func int random_range[int to]

Returns a value in 0..to-1.

10 random_range    // 0..9

/// warning "Not modulo-bias-free" random_range uses modulo, which introduces a slight bias when to is not a power of two. For most uses this is acceptable.

docs.title: prng_randomize_state_xorshift
docs.text:
pub func void prng_randomize_state_xorshift[]

Advances the PRNG state with the Xorshift step. Called by random.

call prng_randomize_state_xorshift

docs.title: std/stringbuilder
docs.text:
A growable string buffer.

#include "std/string_builder"

docs.title: StringBuilder
docs.text:
struct StringBuilder
    data CStr
    len int
    cap int
end
Field Type Description data CStr Buffer pointer len int Current length in bytes cap int Allocated capacity in bytes

docs.title: sb_new
docs.text:
pub func *StringBuilder sb_new[]

Allocates a new StringBuilder with default capacity (SB_DEFAULT_CAP, 1024 bytes) and returns a pointer to it.

var sb *StringBuilder
&sb call sb_new !<

No free

There is no free for a StringBuilder yet. Allocations live until the program exits.

No growth

sb_append does not grow the buffer. Appending more than cap bytes overflows. Check len + sv.len <= cap before appending.

docs.title: sb_append
docs.text:
pub func void sb_append[*StringBuilder sb, *string sv]

Appends a string to the builder. Copies sv.len bytes from sv.data into sb.data at offset sb.len, then advances sb.len.

var sb *StringBuilder
&sb call sb_new !<
sb "hello" call sb_append

docs.title: sb_to_string
docs.text:
pub func void sb_to_string[*StringBuilder sb, *string sv]

Points sv.data at the builder's buffer and sets sv.len to the builder's length.

var sb *StringBuilder
var sv string
&sb call sb_new !<
sb &sv call sb_to_string
sv call println

No ownership transfer

The resulting string points into the builder's buffer. If the builder is modified afterwards, the string changes too. There is no copy.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
var sb *StringBuilder
&sb call sb_new !<

sb "Hello, " call sb_append
sb "World!"  call sb_append

var sv string
sb &sv call sb_to_string
sv call println    // Hello, World!

docs.title: std/string
docs.text:
String conversion helpers.

#include "std/string.gof"

docs.title: Types
docs.text: CStr is a C-string pointer — an alias for *char[].

docs.title: string_to_cstr
docs.text:
pub func CStr string_to_cstr[*string sv]

Returns the underlying C-string pointer of a string.

var s = "hello"
s call string_to_cstr    // *char[]

docs.title: int_to_cstr
docs.text:
pub func CStr int_to_cstr[int num]

Converts an integer to a null-terminated C-string.

42 call int_to_cstr    // "42"

Negative numbers

Negative numbers are not supported. int_to_cstr returns 0 (null pointer) for negative input.

Shared buffer

The result points into a global static buffer. It is overwritten by the next call to int_to_cstr. Copy the result if you need to keep it.

docs.title: Internals
docs.text:
The module uses two global buffers:

var int64_to_cstr_swap_buf char[20]
var int64_to_cstr_buf      char[20]

int_to_cstr writes digits in reverse into the swap buffer, then copies them in order into the output buffer and null-terminates.

#include "std/types"

docs.text:

Used by std/io, std/string, and FFI.

docs.text:
A generic alias for a fixed-size array:

var a Array{T = int, N = 3}    // int[3]

docs.title: Getting started
docs.text:
This tutorial walks you through your first Gofra program. By the end, you will have compiled and run a working binary.

Not installed yet?

See Install Gofra first.

docs.title: Step 1: write a program
docs.text:
Create hello.gof:

#include "std"

func void main[]
    "Hello, World!" println
end

docs.title: Step 2: compile and run
docs.text:
gofra run hello.gof

You should see:

Hello, World!

docs.title: What just happened
docs.text:
• #include "std" includes required println

  • func void main[] declares the entry point.

  • "Hello, World!" pushes a string onto the stack.
  • println pops it and writes it to stdout.
